topic: RT preserves lean mass in deficit
citation: Hunter GR et al. Resistance training conserves fat-free mass and resting energy expenditure following weight loss. Obesity 2008;16(5):1045-51
population: Premenopausal overweight women (BMI 27-30), African- and European-American
intervention_comparison: Diet + resistance training vs diet + aerobic vs diet only
result_effect_uncertainty: FFM RT 46.9->47.2 kg (maintained); AT 45.4->44.4; NT 47.9->46.4. REE fell in AT and NT, not RT. Strength kept only in RT.
limitations_coi: Untrained overweight women, not lifters; n per arm not verified here
verification: PubMed abstract numbers via search summary

topic: RT preserves lean mass in deficit
citation: Geliebter A et al. Effects of strength or aerobic training on body composition, resting metabolic rate, and peak oxygen consumption in obese dieting subjects. Am J Clin Nutr 1997;66(3):557-63
intervention_comparison: Formula diet at 70% of RMR + strength training vs + aerobic (isoenergetic) vs diet only
result_effect_uncertainty: Weight loss ~9.0 kg, no group difference; strength group lost significantly less FFM (p<0.05); RMR fell in all groups equally
limitations_coi: Untrained obese; very large deficit (~5150 kJ/d intake); short

topic: RT preserves lean mass in deficit
citation: Cava E, Yeat NC, Mittendorfer B. Preserving healthy muscle during weight loss. Adv Nutr 2017;8(3):511-519
intervention_comparison: Diet alone vs diet + protein vs diet + endurance/resistance exercise
result_effect_uncertainty: Diet-induced loss reduces muscle mass without hurting strength; high protein helps preserve lean mass but not strength; both endurance and resistance exercise help preserve muscle
limitations_coi: Narrative; obese populations. The often-quoted 'about one-quarter of weight lost is lean' was NOT confirmed in this search

topic: Exercise vs diet for lean mass
citation: Weiss EP et al. Effects of weight loss on lean mass, strength, bone, and aerobic capacity. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2017;49(1):206-217
intervention_comparison: 20% calorie restriction (CR) vs endurance exercise (EX) vs both (CREX), matched ~7% loss
outcome_measure: DXA lean mass, VO2max, strength, bone
result_effect_uncertainty: CR: whole-body lean -~2% (p=0.003), leg lean -~4%; CREX attenuated (~1%, ~2%); EX no loss. VO2max CR -6%, EX +15%
limitations_coi: Endurance not resistance exercise; untrained middle-aged; abstract says strength/bone unchanged but press release claims otherwise
verification: Abstract via search summary; press conflict noted

citation: Murphy C, Koehler K. Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength: a meta-analysis and meta-regression. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2022;32(1):125-137 (online 2021)
intervention_comparison: RT in energy deficit vs RT without deficit
result_effect_uncertainty: Lean mass ES -0.57 (impaired); strength ES -0.31, p=0.28 (not significant). Regression: deficit ~500 kcal/d predicted zero lean gain
limitations_coi: Mostly untrained; deficits estimated not measured; 500 kcal threshold is a regression intercept with wide uncertainty; a 2025 blog critique (mdickens) argues the slope is shallower in experimental groups only
verification: Abstract via search summary + secondary critique; page range from memory, UNVERIFIED

citation: Garthe I, Raastad T, Refsnes PE, Koivisto A, Sundgot-Borgen J. Effect of two different weight-loss rates on body composition and strength and power-related performance in elite athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab 2011;21(2):97-104
population: Elite athletes (Norway), mixed sports, mean ~72-75 kg
intervention_comparison: Slow 0.7%/wk vs fast 1.4%/wk body-weight loss, both with 4 RT sessions/wk
limitations_coi: Small n; SR group trained ~3 wk longer (confound); mixed sexes; DXA hydration effects

citation: Garthe I et al. Long-term effect of weight loss on body composition and performance in elite athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab 2011;21(5)
intervention_comparison: Slow vs fast loss groups at 12 mo
result_effect_uncertainty: No significant between-group differences at 12 months
limitations_coi: Small; loss to follow-up not captured

citation: Mero AA et al. Moderate energy restriction with high protein diet results in healthier outcome in women. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2010;7:4
intervention_comparison: ~1100 kcal/d deficit (1 kg/wk) vs ~550 kcal/d (0.5 kg/wk), both higher protein
result_effect_uncertainty: Authors favoured 0.5 kg/wk; faster arm suggested a more catabolic state; jump improved as fat fell
limitations_coi: Very small; women; not trained lifters. NOTE: this is a women's study, not a sprinter study (task brief conflated it with Huovinen)

citation: Huovinen HT et al. Body composition and power performance improved after weight reduction in male athletes without hampering hormonal balance. J Strength Cond Res 2015;29(1):29-36
intervention_comparison: 750 kcal/d restriction (reduced carb, high protein) vs 300 kcal/d restriction
outcome_measure: Body mass, fat mass, FFM, CMJ, 20-m sprint, hormones
result_effect_uncertainty: Only 750 kcal group lost mass (-2.2 +/- 1.0 kg) and fat (-1.7 +/- 1.6 kg); FFM, testosterone, cortisol unchanged; CMJ +2.6 cm, sprint -0.04 s. 300 kcal group: no significant change
limitations_coi: Very small; 4 wk; deficit and carb reduction confounded. DIRECTLY RELEVANT: a 300 kcal/d deficit produced no measurable fat loss in 4 wk

citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2014;11:20
intervention_comparison: n/a
result_effect_uncertainty: Lose ~0.5-1% body weight/wk; protein 2.3-3.1 g/kg lean mass; fat 15-30% kcal; rest carbs; nutrient timing has little effect
limitations_coi: Narrative; extrapolated from limited data; authors are coaches in the field (no industry funding noted in summary)

citation: Roth C, Schwiete C, Happ K, Rettenmaier L, Schoenfeld BJ, Behringer M. Resistance training volume does not influence lean mass preservation during energy restriction in trained males. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2023;33(1)
duration: 7 wk (1 wk maintenance 45 kcal/kg, 6 wk at 30 kcal/kg)
intervention_comparison: 5 sets/exercise vs 3 sets/exercise; protein 2.8 g/kg FFM
outcome_measure: Lean mass, rectus femoris thickness (ultrasound), body mass
result_effect_uncertainty: Both lost body mass and lean mass; no group difference; no group x time for RF thickness
limitations_coi: Likely underpowered; short; moderate deficit (~0.35 kg/wk per commentary); lean mass loss partly glycogen/water

citation: Willis LH et al. Effects of aerobic and/or resistance training on body mass and fat mass in overweight or obese adults. J Appl Physiol 2012;113(12):1831-7 (STRRIDE AT/RT)
intervention_comparison: RT (3x8-12, 3 d/wk) vs AT (~120 min/wk at ~65-80% VO2peak) vs AT+RT
outcome_measure: Body mass, fat mass, lean mass (DXA/air displacement)
result_effect_uncertainty: AT and AT/RT lost more body and fat mass than RT; AT/RT not better than AT for fat despite ~2x time; lean mass rose in RT and AT/RT not AT
limitations_coi: No diet control; untrained; modalities not energy-matched; high dropout
verification: Abstract via search summary; exact dose numbers from memory, UNVERIFIED

citation: Wewege M, van den Berg R, Ward RE, Keech A. The effects of high-intensity interval training vs moderate-intensity continuous training on body composition in overweight and obese adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Obes Rev 2017;18(6):635-646
intervention_comparison: HIIT vs MICT
result_effect_uncertainty: Both reduced fat mass and waist; no between-modality difference; HIIT ~40% less time; ~2 kg fat, ~3 cm waist over ~10 wk; running, not cycling, drove fat loss
limitations_coi: Untrained obese; few trials; short

citation: Keating SE, Johnson NA, Mielke GI, Coombes JS. A systematic review and meta-analysis of interval training versus moderate-intensity continuous training on body adiposity. Obes Rev 2017;18(8):943-964
intervention_comparison: HIIT/SIT vs MICT
result_effect_uncertainty: No difference on any fat outcome; within-group ~-1.3% (HIIT) vs -1.5% (MICT) body fat; lower-volume protocols trended to favour MICT (p=0.09); neither clinically meaningful short-term
limitations_coi: Short trials; heterogeneous

citation: Viana RB et al. Is interval training the magic bullet for fat loss? A systematic review and meta-analysis comparing MICT with HIIT. Br J Sports Med 2019;53(10):655-664. RETRACTED

result_effect_uncertainty: Claimed 28.5% greater absolute fat-mass loss with interval training; no difference in %fat
limitations_coi: RETRACTED for methodological problems (per BJSM page and Steele 2021). Do not cite as evidence
verification: Retraction status seen on BJSM page via search; reasons not read

citation: Steele J et al. Slow and steady, or hard and fast? A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies comparing body composition changes between interval training and moderate intensity continuous training. Sports 2021;9(11):155
intervention_comparison: Interval vs MICT
result_effect_uncertainty: Fat mass SMD -0.016 (95% CI -0.07 to 0.04), I2 36%; FFM trivial; GRADE certainty high
limitations_coi: Pooled mostly untrained; supersedes Viana

intervention_comparison: Strength only vs endurance only vs concurrent
result_effect_uncertainty: Hypertrophy ES ~1.23 strength-only, ~0.85 concurrent, ~0.27 endurance; running (not cycling) impaired hypertrophy and strength; dose-dependent on cardio frequency and duration
limitations_coi: Older evidence base; small studies; ES values via secondary summary
verification: Effect sizes via secondary summaries; page range from memory, UNVERIFIED

citation: Schumann M et al. Compatibility of concurrent aerobic and strength training for skeletal muscle size and function: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med 2022;52:601-612
intervention_comparison: Concurrent vs strength-only
outcome_measure: Whole-muscle hypertrophy, max strength, explosive strength
result_effect_uncertainty: No compromise of hypertrophy or max strength; explosive strength impaired only when done in same session (p=0.043), not when >=3 h apart; independent of cardio type, frequency, training status
limitations_coi: Most trials short and in untrained/moderately trained; one catalog lists a different first author (Doma) - Schumann as corresponding author confirmed
